title: Merge Intervals
statement: Given an array of intervals where intervals[i] = [start_i, end_i], merge all overlapping intervals and return an array of the non-overlapping intervals covering all input intervals.
constraints: Intervals are not given in sorted order

examples.explanation: The first two intervals overlap and merge into [1,6].
Touching endpoints count as overlapping, so 4 is shared.

hints.content: Interval problems fail when the input is unsorted. What is the first operation that makes everything else easy?
Sort by start. Then every later interval either starts after the current end, or it overlaps the current one.
When two intervals overlap, the merged end is the maximum of the two ends, not the second one you read.
Use > and not >= in the no-overlap check, because [1,4] and [4,5] must merge into [1,5].

pseudocode: if merged is empty or start > last(merged).end:
invariant: merged holds the disjoint answer for every interval processed so far, and its intervals are sorted and never overlap.
whyThisPattern: Once the intervals are sorted by start, a single left to right pass is enough because each interval can only interact with the last merged interval. The pattern is sort, then scan, then ask overlap, then merge.
bruteForce: Repeatedly merging all pairs until nothing changes can take O(n^3) and is hard to reason about. Sorting first reduces the work to O(n log n) for the sort plus a linear scan.
interviewExplanation: I sort the intervals by their start value, then walk them once, keeping the merged result as a list. For each interval I compare its start with the end of the last interval I have already merged: if it starts later there is no overlap and I append it, otherwise I extend the last merged interval to the maximum end. This gives O(n log n) time dominated by the sort.
commonMistakes: Comparing against the previous input interval instead of the last merged interval.
Using >= instead of > in the no-overlap check, which drops the merge of touching intervals.
Setting the merged end to the current end instead of the maximum of the two ends, which can shorten an interval.

animationSteps.title: Sort first
animationSteps.text: Sorting by start turns the problem into one linear scan: 1-3, 2-6, 8-10, 15-18.

animationSteps.title: First interval
animationSteps.description: Nothing to merge with yet, so [1,3] is a new interval.
animationSteps.text: The merged list now contains the interval from 1 to 3.

animationSteps.title: Overlap detected
animationSteps.description: 2 starts before the merged end 3, so the interval merges.
animationSteps.text: The interval from 2 to 6 starts before the merged end of 3, so it overlaps and the merged interval becomes 1 to 6.

animationSteps.title: Predict the move
animationSteps.description: The next interval starts at 8. Overlap or not?
animationSteps.text: The merged interval ends at 6 and the next interval starts at 8. Choose the action.

payload.prompt: merged end = 6, next interval start = 8. What happens?
payload.explanation: 8 is greater than 6, so there is no overlap and a new interval is appended.

animationSteps.title: Final merged list
animationSteps.text: After the scan the result is 1 to 6, 8 to 10 and 15 to 18, which are sorted and non-overlapping.

animationSteps.title: Sorted result
animationSteps.description: One pass after the sort produced the answer.
animationSteps.text: The merged intervals are 1 to 6, 8 to 10 and 15 to 18, produced by a single scan after sorting.

options: Unsorted intervals, each a pair of endpoints
A set of points on a line
breakdown.explanation: Unsorted [start, end] pairs. The order carries no meaning, so something has to put them in line before they can be combined.

options: The total length covered by all intervals
Non-overlapping intervals covering all of the input
breakdown.explanation: A merged set that still covers every input interval. Returning a total length instead would throw away the structure the answer is made of.

breakdown.prompt: When do two intervals count as overlapping?
options: Only when one sits strictly inside the other
When the next start is at or before the current end
Only when they share an endpoint exactly
breakdown.explanation: Touching counts as overlap, since intervals are continuous. So if the next start is less than or equal to where the current one ends, the two are one interval with the later end.
